And it goes back to the Shelby decision in 2013. When the Supreme Court said in a nutshell, and I paraphrase obviously, we are not saying that there is no discrimination in this country. But we do not believe that you can prove that there's discrimination based upon a formula that you have been using for 40 years. Because at that time, if you lived in, and they were primarily southern states admittedly, if you, let's say if you lived in the state of Alabama, in order for you to make any major changes, even as to closing polling places or moving them, you had to get permission from the justice apartment of the federal government. so that we could be sure that whether it be your intent, but that the effect would not be discriminatory or would not suppress the vote. And so once Shelby's decision was rendered, there were some 26 states within a matter of days. that changed their laws. So that's when you started seeing the voter ID laws. That's when you started seeing large numbers of polling places closed and or moved. That's when you started seeing other impediments to voting put in people's way. That's when they wanted to ask the citizenship questions. That's when they wanted, you just use, like I said, certain forms of ID. So all of those things came as a result of the Shelby decision by the United States Supreme Court. What we did from my committee is we traveled around the country to get the evidence that the Supreme Court said we did not have, so that we could put in place a new formula based upon contemporary data. And so what we did was put together a document showing that in fact, there is still discrimination. There are still voter suppression efforts, and it is worse even than it was in 1965. I mean, the State of Ohio should be included. Places in New York should be included. Places in Wisconsin should be included. It's almost judged when you say, be careful what you ask for, because that data now exists. So what we are faced with is the first major election in our history, in recent history, without the protections of the Voting Rights Act. And that is why these states and these localities are doing whatever they feel like doing. And that's why we're suing them, whether it be in Texas or in Wisconsin or in Alabama.
